儲君 is the designated heir, not a 'stored lord'; 節 here is the speaker's proper measure/role, as the idiomatic already shows.

English grammar is broken ('the position emperor of China'); 皇帝位 is the imperial position, not a unique 'emperor of China' title in the Chinese.

He appointed Murong Ke as grand steward, with authority to record the affairs of the Masters of Writing, performing the Duke of Zhou's duties;
錄尚書 is the regent's control of secretariat business, not 'recording secretary affairs'.

Moyu Gen, swaggering on old merit, resented Murong Ke's power and plotted usurpation. He told Ke, "The boy emperor and meddling dowager invite a coup like Yang Jun's or Zhuge Yuansun's—you must secure yourself.
諸葛元遜 is the courtesy name of Zhuge Ke, not Zhuge Dan (諸葛誕). The English invents the wrong referent.

抑亦 means 'and yet also / nonetheless also', not 'suppress'.

exhausted picked crack is unintelligible; 盡精銳 is committing all crack troops.

‘wang-zuo’ is an untranslated calque of 王佐; the English is otherwise unintelligible.

洛州 is Luozhou, not Luoyang; the sentence is also ungrammatical as English.

Military discipline should be made strict, relief granted first, soldiers trained and taught battle so squads have fixed assignments; beyond campaigning they should have enough to manage private livelihoods—if fathers and elder brothers have Mount Di to look upon and sons and younger brothers harbor thoughts of Confucius's care, though sent through fire and water, what would they not follow!

Military discipline should be made strict, relief granted first, soldiers trained and taught battle so squads have fixed assignments; beyond campaigning they should have enough to manage private livelihoods—if fathers and elder brothers have the Mount Di gaze of the Odes and sons and younger brothers harbor that close familial care, though sent through fire and water, what would they not follow!
孔爾之顧 parallels 陟岵 as a Shijing kinship idiom (close/cherishing care), not a mention of Confucius; the idiomatic English invents a named person.
Fu Jian sent Wang Meng against Huguan and Yang An against Jinyang.
Fu Jian again sent Wang Meng and Yang An leading a host to campaign against Murong Wei; Wang Meng attacked Huguan, Yang An attacked Jinyang.
The idiomatic English drops 又, the joint dispatch 率眾伐暐, and the personal object 暐, collapsing two coordinated commanders into a looser pair of attacks.

If nobles below the rank of duke take the four seas as home, reward and punishment are trusted and enforced, and discipline is upheld—Huan Wen's head could hang from a white banner and the rulers of Qin and Wu could be brought to submit by ritual; would that not only stop their invasions!

If nobles below the rank of duke take the four seas as home, reward and punishment are trusted and enforced, and discipline is upheld—the heads of Wen and Meng could hang from a white banner and the rulers of Qin and Wu could be brought to submit by ritual; would that not only stop their invasions!
Chinese 溫、猛之首 enumerates two heads; the idiomatic English keeps only Huan Wen and omits 猛.

Ping's nature was greedy and base; he blocked mountain springs, sold firewood and water, piled cash and silk like hills and mounds—the three armies had none fighting will.

「潞川」 is the Lu River, not a truncated 'the Lu', and 「評等單騎遁還」 is plural flight, not Ping alone.

「堅將巨武」 is Jian's general, not an unnamed Qin soldier.

「壽春」 is Shouchun, not Shouzhou, and the sentence omits 別部都督.

Chinese 昨拜今卿 describes Huangfu Zhen's shift as seen by Wang Meng, not Wang Meng bowing or using a personal name of himself.

Yuanzhen looked like Heaven's chosen: deep, resolute, and full of stratagems.
元真 is Murong Huang's courtesy name; the Gui section has already closed.
While rivals contended, a child emperor sat in Jin and Yu Liang hijacked the regency—Murong Gui seized the moment of Jin's weakness.
While rivals contended, Mingzong performed the sacrifices in childhood and Yu Liang, the senior maternal uncle, hijacked the regency—Yuanzhen seized the moment of Jin's weakness.
The subject continues 元真 (Murong Huang). 顯宗 is named, and 元舅 is Yu Liang's kinship to that emperor.
Murong Wei, a mediocrity, left rule to ministers while foes stalled at Hangu and easterners died at Ye.

Jingmao, a mediocrity who did not attend to affairs himself, relied on worthy aides while rebellious ministers thwarted plans; then Jinyong fell and Henan submitted, the bronze-walled city was embraced and the desert north faced, Western Qin's crack troops halted at Hangu, and the remnant people of the eastern Xia looked to the palace at Ye and surrendered.
The idiomatic line invents 'died at Ye' for 授首 (surrender) and drops Jingmao's courtesy name plus the Jinyong, Henan, bronze city, desert-north, and rebellious-minister clauses.

Jingmao was mediocre stuff, not personally attending to affairs; worthy assistants were relied on; rebellious ministers thwarted plans—thereupon fell Jinyong and treated Henan, wrapped the bronze-walled city and faced the desert north, west Qin's crack troops halted at Hangu and did not advance, eastern Xia's surviving black-haired gazed at Ye palace and handed heads.

Jingmao was mediocre stuff, not personally attending to affairs; worthy assistants were relied on; rebellious ministers thwarted plans—thereupon Jinyong fell and Henan submitted, the bronze-walled city was embraced and the desert north faced, west Qin's crack troops halted at Hangu and did not advance, eastern Xia's surviving black-haired gazed at Ye palace and handed over their heads.
款河南 is submission/opening of Henan, not 'treated Henan'.
Like Youyu's defection that destroyed Qin or Zichang's treason that ruined Chu, they died abroad unable to save themselves—proof that fate follows conduct.
Like Youyu's departure that destroyed the Rong or Zichang's rise that overturned Ying, they died abroad unable to save themselves—proof that fate follows conduct.
由餘出而戎亡 is Youyu leaving and the Rong perishing, not Qin's destruction; 子常升而郢覆 is Zichang's rise and Ying's fall, not a stated treason against Chu.

unresolvedReferences.description: 帝 / the emperor who dispatched Huan Wen is not named; recorded as p024 and not equated with 穆帝 (p018).
Yewang siege dated only 自三月至八月 after Jun's death; calendar year not stated in this chunk.
The prophecy 燕馬當飲渭水 names no individual.
區區僭豎 is a collective slur for Qin usurpers, not a named person.
猛 enumerated with 溫 as a head that could hang is not given a surname or office; identity remains open and is treated as distinct from later 王猛.
秦、吳二主 are title-only; Wu ruler is never named. Qin ruler is aligned with later 苻堅 by narrative role, not by an explicit same-name statement.
Qin's summoned envoy (其使) is an unnamed office-holder and was not turned into a person.
